## Executive Summary

**Problem.** The global deployment of Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) in 2026 is gated less by reactor design maturity than by a single, fragile input: High-Assay Low-Enriched Uranium (HALEU, enrichment 5–20% U-235) [19]. Today only Russia and China operate HALEU-scale enrichment infrastructure, while the U.S., EU, and UK are racing to build sovereign capacity in the face of import bans, licensing gaps, and container-transport bottlenecks [19][27]. Without a mapped, resilient supply chain, SMR operators face fuel-assembly delays, cost overruns, and deployment slippage that would undermine their LCOE competitiveness against solar+storage.

**Key systems.** Three interlocking systems define the 2026 landscape:

1. **Enrichment & conversion cascade** — HALEU requires dedicated centrifuges, new de-conversion/denitration lines, and modified transport casks; current LEU (<5%) infrastructure cannot be trivially up-rated [19][27].
2. **Reactor fleet & fuel licensing** — The NEA SMR Dashboard tracks six non-technical readiness dimensions (licensing, siting, financing, supply chain, engagement, fuel), showing that fuel remains the weakest link across most designs [7].
3. **LCOE economics** — EIA AEO2025 estimates for 2030 online plants use a 30-year cost recovery period and 6.65% after-tax WACC, providing a standardized benchmark for SMR vs. solar+storage comparison [5].

**Main findings.** 2026 marks a pivot from “HALEU scarcity” to “HALEU logistics.” Centrus Energy has produced over 920 kg of HALEU at Piketon, Ohio (Oct 2023–mid-2025), and the U.S. NNSA–Japan MEXT/JAEA partnership delivered the largest-ever HALEU shipment to U.S. industry — but this volume is measured in tonnes, while a single 300 MWe SMR fleet needs hundreds of tonnes per year [19][27].
